title: Grabovica and Uzdol: ARBiH Atrocities During Operation Neretva 93
content:
Operation Neretva 93, launched in September 1993, was one of the ARBiH's most ambitious offensives of the war -- an attempt to break through HVO lines in Herzegovina and relieve pressure on besieged Bosniak populations in Mostar and the Neretva River valley. The operation involved units drawn from multiple corps, including elite formations transferred from the Sarajevo front. It was during this offensive that ARBiH soldiers committed two massacres of Croat civilians that would result in the indictment of the operation's nominal commander, ARBiH Chief of Staff Sefer Halilovic, before the ICTY.

On 8-9 September 1993, soldiers from ARBiH units killed Croat civilians in the village of Grabovica, located along the Neretva River south of Jablanica. The ICTY Halilovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-48-T) established that at least thirteen civilians were killed in Grabovica, including women and elderly residents. The victims were local Croat villagers in whose homes ARBiH soldiers had been billeted. The killings were not the result of combat but deliberate acts against a defenseless civilian population.

On 14 September, a separate ARBiH unit attacked the Croat village of Uzdol in the municipality of Prozor. The ICTY trial record documented the deaths of at least twenty-nine civilians and one captured HVO soldier. The attack on Uzdol, like Grabovica, targeted a village that posed no military threat. Houses were burned and livestock killed in what amounted to a punitive raid against a civilian settlement.

The Halilovic trial addressed a complex question of command responsibility. Halilovic had been designated to coordinate Operation Neretva 93, and the prosecution argued that he exercised effective control over the units involved. The Trial Chamber, however, acquitted Halilovic in November 2005, finding that the prosecution had not established beyond reasonable doubt that he possessed the effective command authority necessary for superior responsibility under international humanitarian law. The judgment noted the confused and overlapping command arrangements within the ARBiH during this period, where formal titles did not always correspond to actual authority over forces in the field.

The acquittal did not diminish the established facts of what occurred at Grabovica and Uzdol. The Trial Chamber's findings of fact regarding the killings themselves were detailed and unambiguous. What the judgment addressed was the specific legal question of whether Halilovic, as opposed to other commanders, bore criminal liability for failing to prevent or punish the crimes.

For the broader trajectory of the war, the Grabovica and Uzdol massacres carried significant consequences. They undermined the Bosnian government's moral position at a time when international sympathy was a critical strategic asset. The crimes provided ammunition to those who argued that all sides in the Bosnian conflict bore equivalent responsibility for atrocities -- a framing that the Bosnian government vigorously contested but found increasingly difficult to counter when its own forces committed documented war crimes.

The massacres also deepened the hostility between Bosniak and Croat communities in Herzegovina, hardening positions on both sides of a conflict that was already producing its own cycle of atrocity and retaliation. Operation Neretva 93 achieved limited military objectives, but the crimes committed during its execution left scars that outlasted the fighting itself. Grabovica and Uzdol remain painful evidence that the capacity for violence against civilians was not confined to any single faction in the Bosnian War.
